changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For operations buyers (COO-level) with peak events, answer the question 'who's my person' with a name, not a tier table. Suggested line: 'A name, not a queue: a named account lead and solutions engineer, a shared channel, and a clear escalation path for your biggest days.' Use this only where we can actually staff it, and keep tiers and response times as backup detail, not the headline.
changes.why: When Halima asked 'who's my person' she was walked through tiers and response times and called it 'a queue with a faster timer', while the competitor brought a named solutions engineer and account lead.

changes.change: Add a peak-event line for ticketing and other on-sale buyers that leads with the response, not uptime: 'You don't buy uptime, you buy what happens when it's down: who is watching on your on-sale morning, who you call, and what happens in the first minutes.' Keep uptime and throughput stats as supporting proof underneath.
changes.why: The decider said 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down', and the evaluation began with a failure plus a ticket-form support reply that came 'after the on-sale was over', not with throughput.

changes.change: Create a proof asset to sit behind the support message: a one-page on-sale runbook showing, on paper, what we do on an on-sale morning (who is watching, who the customer calls, what happens at minute four). Reps and SEs build it with the customer before the decision meeting.
changes.why: Halima wanted to see 'on paper, what we do on an on-sale morning', the rep said 'We don't have that as a thing', and admits one could have been built with the SE.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For peak-event buyers, add a referenceable customer (ideally in ticketing) who will speak directly about who picked up during a high-traffic event, offered as a call, not just a logo or story.
changes.why: The rep's own diagnosis was 'I had logos. I didn't have a person.', and the buyer's criterion was 'Someone who picks up.'
